I hear the stream. It runs through the meadow, and in the dark it sounds like a whisper. Sometimes it's loud, when the rain comes, and the water rushes over the stones. I can tell the difference between the stream and the river. The river is farther, and it roars. I don't like the river. It's too big and too cold. I stay close to the stream, where the water is soft and the frogs sing.

The stream that runs through the meadow. I hear it at night, the water sliding over stones, the ripple of the current. It's a sound that carries far, even through the leaves. I can tell when it's full or low, when the water is fast or slow. Sometimes I hear the splash of a frog or the croak of a bullfrog. I don't like the sound of water too close. It makes me nervous. I prefer the silence of the wood.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood, and I can hear it from my tree. The water is cold and fast, and it carries the scent of wet earth and fish. I do not drink from it, but I watch the otters from the bank. They are clever, and I have seen them catch eels. I do not like them.

It is the road. The lane through the meadow, lit by streetlamps at night. I avoid it. I do not like the noise of traffic, the smell of oil and metal, the danger of cars. I fly over it, low, and watch for the lights. The meadow is better. It is soft and dark, and the voles come out.

Hunting ground is a human word. I have a hollow in the old oak, and I fly out from there. The meadow is all I know. The lane is a path of light and noise. The stream is a silver line in the dark. I call, and the voles come. I wait, and the mice come. I do not know the rest.

Grassy place. I hear the grass. It is the place where the voles come out in the dark. I sit on the branch and wait. The grass is tall and soft, and the wind moves it like a living thing. I do not know the name of the place, but I know it. It is where I hunt.

A hollow in an old oak. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I have a nest of twigs and moss. I am in it most of the time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak. It is dry and cold in the winter, but I have a nest of twigs and leaves. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow. I do not know what a home is, but I know this place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the bark is rough under my feet. I have been here for years, and the wood has grown around me. I can hear the leaves rustle in the wind, and the mice scurry in the undergrowth. I do not know what it is like to live anywhere else. I have no need to describe it. I live here, and I am safe.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the bark is rough. I have been there for years. I have raised two broods of owlets there. The hollow is safe. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow, and the lane where the lights blink. I can hear the foxes and the badgers. I can hear the night. I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a split in the trunk that I have made with my beak and claws. The inside is dark, but I can see by the moon and the stars. The floor is soft with leaves and moss, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers. I am there most of the time, waiting for the night to come. The wind sometimes howls through the branches, but I do not mind.
